input:
A centrifugal pump is used to move water between two vessels that are located at grade, that is to say, at ground level, so that no static lift between the two vessels enters into the duty that the pump is required to meet. At the duty point of the pump, which is the point at which it is intended to operate, the flow rate delivered is 70 m3 h-1, and this flow is delivered against a head of 32 m. The efficiency of the pump at this operating point is 74%.

The shaft power that is required at the duty point is 8.2 kW. In line with normal practice, the motor that drives the pump is rated somewhat higher than this figure, in fact 15% above the shaft power at the duty point, so that the motor is not obliged to run continuously at the very limit of its rating when the pump is at its duty point.

During the acceptance test that was carried out on the pump, no cavitation was observed. It is important to note, however, that the acceptance test ran for a duration of 4 h and that it covered the duty point only. The absence of cavitation is therefore established for the conditions of that test, and it should not automatically be assumed to extend to other conditions, such as different flows or suction arrangements, that were not part of the test programme.
target:
A centrifugal pump moves water between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 70 m3 h-1 against a head of 32 m, with a pump efficiency of 74%.

The duty point is the operating point the pump is selected for, and the three figures belong together: the flow and the head state what the pump delivers, and the efficiency states what that delivery costs in power. Shaft power at the duty point is 8.2 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value. That margin is part of the specification, not a reserve discovered afterwards: the drive is sized so that continuous operation at the duty point sits inside its rating, with the rating held above the shaft requirement at the one point where the pump is required to run.

Efficiency enters the result directly. At a fixed flow and head, the hydraulic power is fixed, and the shaft power is that hydraulic power divided by the efficiency; a pump of lower efficiency at the same duty point would draw more shaft power to deliver the same flow against the same head.

Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, and the test record is the whole of the evidence on the point. The test ran for 4 h and covered the duty point only. The result is a detection statement at one operating point: no cavitation over that test at the duty point. Running at other flows, or with a lower suction level than the test arrangement provided, is outside the evidence, and the test says nothing about it.
